Cote d'Ivoire: Ivory Coast Cocoa Output Could Fall 25% As El Niño Threatens Harvest
11 November 2026
Daba Finance (Abidjan)
Ivory Coast's cocoa production could decline by 21% to 25% during the 2026-27 season as an El Niño weather event threatens rainfall and crop development, according to the country's national meteorological agency. The warning, reported on November 11, 2026, comes as the world's largest cocoa producer faces reduced harvests and lower deliveries to exporters. The country produced more than 2 million metric tons of cocoa last season, meaning a decline of this scale could remove hundreds of thousands of tons from global supply.
The National Meteorology Directorate of SODEXAM warned that rainfall could fall by 10% to 27%, with a shorter rainy season, longer dry periods and higher temperatures affecting cocoa-growing regions. The agency described the 2026-27 El Niño as a weather event that could rank among the strongest recorded if Pacific Ocean warming continues. Reduced rainfall and heat could damage cocoa trees, cause flowers and young pods to fall, and lower crop yields. The effects could also disrupt planting schedules and reduce water available for agriculture and electricity generation.

titre: Texas citrus undersized, but yield outlook good as harvest begins
texte:
The 2026-2027 Texas citrus harvest is underway, but shipments are running well behind last season after an extremely hot, dry summer kept fruit from sizing up so far, according to a Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service expert.
Juan Anciso, Ph.D., AgriLife Extension vegetable specialist, professor and associate head of AgriLife Extension in the Texas A&M Department of Horticultural Sciences at the Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center at Weslaco, said growers have started harvesting grapefruit, early oranges and navel oranges.
Shipments of both grapefruit and early oranges bound for fresh fruit aisles are at less than half of last year’s pace, Anciso said. As of Oct. 24, the Rio Grande Valley had shipped 80,445 40-pound cartons of fresh fruit this season, compared with 219,613 at the same point last year. Those totals do not include citrus fruit going to juice.
“It’s kind of complex, but I would say the primary culprit is the drought,” he said. “We were very dry this summer, so fruit sizes in oranges, even early oranges, and of course grapefruits, haven’t sized up.”
There was virtually no rain in June, July and August, Anciso said, and the Rio Grande Valley endured intense heat for months with extended consecutive days above 100 degrees. Meaningful rains did not arrive until September and October.

texte:
Cote d'Ivoire: Ivory Coast Rubber Production Hits 2m Tons As Farmers Shift From Cocoa
10 November 2026
Daba Finance (Abidjan)
Ivory Coast's natural rubber production rose to approximately 2 million metric tons in 2025 from 1.8 million tons in 2024, an increase of 11.1%, as more farmers shifted from cocoa cultivation to rubber. The Association of Natural Rubber Professionals of Côte d'Ivoire (APROMAC) announced the figures during an industry event in Abidjan. The country has become Africa's largest rubber producer and ranks second worldwide behind Thailand, according to the association.
APROMAC expects production to remain around 2 million tons in 2026 as the industry focuses on improving product quality and processing capacity. The association's president, Charles-Emmanuel Yacé, said the country has about 50 rubber processing plants with combined capacity exceeding 2 million tons annually. The facilities process latex collected from plantations into rubber products used by manufacturers, including tire producers. Ivory Coast's rubber industry has expanded from 164,138 tons in 2005, increasing output more than 12 times over 20 years.
The expansion has been supported by farmers switching from cocoa to rubber in search of more stable incomes. Rubber trees can provide latex for years once they reach maturity, allowing farmers to generate revenue through repeated harvesting. titre: Citrus harvest forecast to fall 20% to 1.8 million tons in Morocco
texte:
Make us your Google favorite
Morocco's citrus harvest is expected to decline by 20 per cent in the 2026-2027 season, reaching approximately 1.8 million tons compared with 2.2 million tons last season, according to Kacem Bennani Smires, president of Maroc Citrus.
Summer temperatures reaching 46°C caused flower and young fruit drop, while flooding in the Gharb region and alternate bearing further affected yields. Small citrus fruit output is expected to decrease by 15 per cent, including a 20 per cent decline for clementines and 6 per cent for Nadorcott.
Despite lower volumes, exports are forecast at nearly 540,000 tons, down 7 per cent. Larger fruit sizes, supported by lower fruit loads and improved water availability, are expected to increase the proportion suitable for export.
The European Union accounts for nearly 38 per cent of Moroccan citrus exports, followed by Russia at 17%, Canada and the U.S. at 15% each, and Africa at 12 to 14%.
Growers continue to face rising input costs, labor shortages, and competition from Egypt and Turkey. Morocco has also lost nearly 34,000 hectares of citrus orchards over the past decade, with future recovery dependent on irrigation infrastructure development.

titre: El Nino could cut Ivory Coast cocoa production by up to a quarter

El Nino could cut Ivory Coast cocoa production by up to a quarter
Tuesday 10 November 2026 - 13:44pm
ABIDJAN - Cocoa production in Ivory Coast, the world's leading producer, could fall by up to a quarter due to the exceptionally strong El Nino weather phenomenon, meteorologists warned in a note seen by AFP Tuesday.
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds and rainfall patterns, on top of man-made global warming.
It is expected to peak in December but the human impact of its associated extreme temperatures, floods and droughts is set to last into 2027 and beyond.
Ivory Coast's public meteorology body, Sodexam, said it estimated that the climate episode would lead to lower rainfall, higher temperatures and a longer dry season in the west African country.
A water deficit and high temperatures may cut cocoa production "in the order of 21 percent to 25 percent" because of the shrivelling and premature drop of young pods and defoliation of trees, it said in a note notably for the Ivorian government.
The lower production could result in "a colossal loss of income for growers" and in a decline in the state's export revenues, it added.
The country is responsible for nearly 40 percent of global cocoa output, while the crop accounts for 15 percent of GDP, supporting roughly five million people in a country of more than 33 million.

Un protocole d’accord d’achat entre la Cameroon Golden Cocoa et la société Cocoa Valley fixant à 1800 F le kilogramme a été signé hier à Yaoundé.
C’est une ambiance particulièrement festive qui a prévalu hier dans la salle de conférences du ministère du Commerce (Mincommerce). A l’origine, une bonne nouvelle venant de la société Cocoa Valley : le prix du cacao labélisé « Golden Cocoa » est fixé à 1800F le kilogramme. Bien plus cher payé que les 1000F par Kg bord champs actuellement en vigueur sur le marché. Une résolution qui a été matérialisée par un protocole d’accord signé hier entre Wah Lietmbouo Moussa, représentant de ladite société et André Marie Floret Edzigui, directeur général de Cameroon Golden Cocoa. LAGOS, November 7, 2026 (Naija247news) — Nigeria’s cocoa industry faces renewed revenue uncertainty as global cocoa futures fall to a one-month low, with prices declining by as much as 5.2% in New York amid rising exchange inventories, weaker chocolate demand and improving near-term supply conditions.
The price decline introduces a fresh challenge for Nigeria’s agricultural export sector, which has increasingly looked to cocoa as a source of non-oil foreign-exchange earnings and an opportunity to expand domestic agro-processing.
New York’s most actively traded cocoa contract dropped as much as 5.2%, while London futures also declined. The sell-off followed an increase in exchange-monitored inventories in the United States and London, suggesting that immediate supply pressures are easing.
For Nigerian cocoa producers, exporters and processors, the changing international market presents a difficult combination: lower global prices could moderate export earnings, while adverse weather conditions across West Africa threaten production volumes.
The development is particularly important for Nigeria as it seeks to strengthen agricultural exports, diversify foreign-exchange receipts and capture more value from its commodity production.

Implemented by BAFF Livelihoods under HDFC Bank's Parivartan initiative from January 2022 to March 2025, the project brought 1,200 rural families into organised orange cultivation. Technical guidance, improved farming practices and sustained efforts have helped orchards flourish.

titre: Drought cuts citrus yields in Montenegro's Ulcinj region
texte:
Make us your Google favorite
Prolonged drought and high temperatures have affected citrus cultivation in Montenegro's Ulcinj region, where the harvest is expected to reach 6,000 to 7,000 tons from approximately 350,000 mandarin, orange, and lemon trees.
Ghani Redža, an advisor at the municipal Secretariat for Agriculture, Rural Development and Ecology, said the region experienced approximately four months without rainfall, affecting fruit quality and yields.
"Where the producers had irrigation systems, there was also production, but not in the sense that it was regular. So, for example, with mandarins, the crop is weaker in both quantity and quality compared to last year," said Redža.
Growers face higher input and labor costs, while citrus selling prices remain at last year's levels. Marketing and labor availability also present challenges.
Pomegranate and fig yields are estimated at 500 to 600 tons. Watermelon growers harvested around 4,000 tons, with the entire crop reportedly sold.
Government subsidies amount to approximately €300 (US$350) per hectare. Municipal support includes seed and irrigation subsidies, alongside funding covering 50% of equipment purchase costs.

titre: Florida citrus harvest forecast to fall 19 percent
texte:
Make us your Google favorite
Florida's citrus harvest is forecast to decline by nearly 19 per cent in the 2026/27 season, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). Orange output is expected to fall by 23 per cent, grapefruit by 4 per cent, and tangerines and tangelos by 2 per cent. Lemon volumes are projected to increase by 6 per cent.
Orange growers are expected to harvest 10 million 90-pound boxes, including 7 million boxes of Valencia oranges. Grapefruit volumes are forecast at 1.3 million boxes, while tangerines and tangelos are projected at 450,000 boxes. Lemon output is estimated at 950,000 boxes.
Florida Citrus Mutual attributes part of the decline to two winter freezes earlier this year. Citrus greening disease, hurricanes, and land development continue to affect the sector.
The USDA's August inventory showed citrus acreage had declined by 21 per cent year on year to approximately 66,773 hectares across 23 counties, down 73 per cent from two decades ago.
Florida's current state budget allocates US$196 million to the citrus industry, including US$160 million for new plantings and citrus greening treatments. Growers are also seeking US$3.5 billion in federal freeze disaster assistance.

A study of crop yields in tropical cocoa-growing regions finds that increasing bouts of drought and deluge pose a substantial threat to cocoa harvests. Researchers led by Anna Lea Albright ’17, A.M. ’17, and professor of environmental science and engineering Peter Huybers combined decades of cocoa production records with daily weather data from Ghana, Ecuador, and Indonesia. They found that unusually heavy rain during flowering and early pod development was consistently associated with lower yields. In Ghana, heavy wet-season rain together with dry-season drought explained nearly 70 percent of year-to-year variation in production.

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia is eyeing an expansion of its cocoa production for higher-value chocolate products and to reduce import dependence, an official said on Saturday.
Expanding cocoa cultivation in the northern Borneo states of Sarawak and Sabah, the country's main cocoa-producing states, could increase local raw material supplies, Shari Fuddin Sha'ari, acting director-general of the Malaysian Cocoa Board, said at the launch of "A Malaysian Cocoa Affair 2026."
"We hope increased local production will help narrow the supply gap for dried cocoa beans from overseas. This will also create greater economic opportunities for farmers and entrepreneurs through the production of downstream products," he said.
Shari Fuddin said the board is pioneering chocolate production using Sarawak cocoa beans through a single-origin approach, with dried beans from four locations processed at a cluster cooperative research center in Sarawak.

titre: Candy Makers Face Higher Cocoa Prices and Tighter Sugar Supplies
texte:
GREENWOOD VILLAGE, Colo. (RFD-TV) — Candy makers are paying more for cocoa while facing tighter sugar availability this year.
CoBank Analyst Billy Roberts says cocoa prices are well above where they were last year at this time.
“As recently as March or April of this year, we’ve seen those cocoa prices kind of trend down to about the $3,000 per ton level on New York futures trading. Those prices started to increase a bit more once some concerns started to surface about this year’s harvest and especially once concerns about the El Nino weather pattern that started to emerge really started to take hold in the industry and influence what some of those futures traders were expecting in terms of this year’s harvest.”
Roberts says candy makers are also dealing with challenges surrounding this year’s sugar crop.
“Drought-related reductions in planted acreage of sugar beets, some relatively lower sugar prices have impacted growers, a lot of high input costs which are impacting pretty much every facet of the ingredient supply chain, and some uncertainty overall in the sugar space about sugar demand from consumers because a lot of concern there stems from consumers’ continued embrace of GLP-1s. Regardless, it’s still impacting the amount of sugar that’s actually available on the market.”
Pests have created another challenge for sugar this year, with the pasture mealybug taking a big bite out of Louisiana fields.

titre: Heat and drought reduce grapefruit size in Texas
texte:
Make us your Google favorite
Citrus growers in Texas' Rio Grande Valley are reporting smaller fruit sizes as harvesting begins, following a summer of high temperatures and limited rainfall.
Michael Flowers, Field Operations Manager at Lone Star Citrus, said heat stress and insufficient soil moisture have affected fruit development.
"We need water to grow, but 96 days of triple digits is painful for everything. So with the mix of lack of water, we are having size issues," Flowers said.
Growers are using sizing rings in orchards to assess fruit readiness. Although smaller grapefruit are expected early in the harvest season, Flowers said current sizing remains below expectations, leaving some fruit unsuitable for harvesting.
According to the National Weather Service, McAllen recorded 101 days with temperatures reaching at least 100°F (37.8°C), exceeding the previous record of 97 days in 2023.
Meteorologist Barry Goldsmith explained that brief rainfall periods do not necessarily restore soil moisture, as deficits can return within weeks.
The smaller grapefruit crop could also reduce demand for harvest labor. Flowers noted that prolonged heat and dry conditions are becoming a recurring challenge for citrus growers in the region.

titre: Brazilian orange crop forecast at 263.2 million boxes as juice prices fall
texte:

Brazil's orange juice market is facing lower demand as the 2026/27 season begins, with prices declining despite expectations of a smaller orange crop, according to a Mintec analysis published on October 1, 2026.
Fundecitrus forecasts the São Paulo and West-Southwest Minas Gerais citrus belt will harvest 263.2 million boxes of 40.8 kg in 2026/27. The forecast is 3.1% above the May estimate but around 10.2% below the 2025/26 season. Citrus greening disease, or HLB, continues to contribute to fruit drop across the main growing region.
© Expana
Despite the lower supply forecast, orange juice prices have been declining since March. Expana Benchmark Prices for orange concentrate FCA Europe stood at US$2,200 per ton on September 30, down 7% month on month.
Market participants attribute weaker demand to high retail prices and large frozen concentrated orange juice (FCOJ) inventories. Some sources report lower sales as consumers switch to alternative products, while others point to changing consumption patterns related to the sugar content of orange juice.
Some market participants say current price levels are putting pressure on grower returns, with raw material prices being calculated backward from lower sales prices. Attention is now focused on new contracts between bottlers and retailers, with lower retail prices viewed by market participants as a factor in any recovery in demand.

Source: Citi Newsroom
The government has increased the producer price of cocoa at the farm gate from GH¢41,392 per tonne to GH¢42,400 per tonne for the 2026/2027 crop season.
The new price gives farmers a GH¢1,008 increase over the previous price. It also translates into GH¢2,650 for a 64-kilogramme bag of cocoa and represents 71.18 per cent of the realised gross free-on-board (FOB) price.
The Chief Executive of the Ghana Cocoa Board (COCOBOD),Randy Abbey, announced the new producer price in Accra last Friday and declared the 2026/2027 cocoa crop season open.
The new price was set under the newly enacted Ghana Cocoa Board Act, 2026 (Act 1182), which guarantees cocoa farmers a minimum of 70 per cent of the realised gross FOB price.
Existing rates and fees for other participants in the cocoa supply chain, including buyers' margins, hauliers’ rates, warehousing and internal marketing costs, as well as charges for grading, sealing and disinfestation, have been maintained.
He said the new price had been agreed following consultations with COCOBOD, the Ministry of Finance, cocoa farmers and stakeholders represented by the Chamber of Cocoa Marketers, including licensed buying companies, haulage companies and processors.

Cocoa: Price of 64-kg per bag increases from GH¢2,587 to GH¢2,650 for 2026/2027 crop season
Samuel Ohene Ewur
Business News
Sep - 28 - 2026 , 07:33
The government has increased the producer price of cocoa at the farm gate from GH¢41,392 per tonne to GH¢42,400 per tonne for the 2026/2027 crop season.
The new price gives farmers a GH¢1,008 increase over the previous price. It also translates into GH¢2,650 for a 64-kilogramme bag of cocoa and represents 71.18 per cent of the realised gross free-on-board (FOB) price.
The Chief Executive of the Ghana Cocoa Board (COCOBOD),Randy Abbey, announced the new producer price in Accra last Friday and declared the 2026/2027 cocoa crop season open.
The new price was set under the newly enacted Ghana Cocoa Board Act, 2026 (Act 1182), which guarantees cocoa farmers a minimum of 70 per cent of the realised gross FOB price.
Existing rates and fees for other participants in the cocoa supply chain, including buyers' margins, hauliers’ rates, warehousing and internal marketing costs, as well as charges for grading, sealing and disinfestation, have been maintained.
He said the new price had been agreed following consultations with COCOBOD, the Ministry of Finance, cocoa farmers and stakeholders represented by the Chamber of Cocoa Marketers, including licensed buying companies, haulage companies and processors.

Dr Ransford Abbey, CE of COCOBOD
The Ghana Cocoa Board (COCOBOD) has announced a new producer price of GH¢42,400 per tonne of cocoa for the 2026/2027 crop season, translating into GH¢2,650 per 64-kilogramme bag.
The new price takes effect today, Friday, September 25, 2026, according to a statement issued by COCOBOD.
COCOBOD said cocoa farmers would receive 71.18 per cent of the realised gross Free on Board (FOB) value under the new pricing arrangement.
The Board also reaffirmed its commitment to maintaining the premium quality of Ghana’s cocoa as the new crop season gets underway.
At the announced rate, a farmer will receive GH¢2,650 for every 64kg bag of cocoa sold, while a tonne will attract GH¢42,400.
The producer price is the amount paid to farmers for their cocoa and is reviewed at the beginning of crop seasons.
COCOBOD’s announcement did not provide a breakdown of the realised gross FOB value or the factors used to arrive at the 71.18 per cent farmer share.
The new producer price applies from September 25, 2026, for the 2026/2027 crop season.

titre: Cocoa prices hit record highs in 2024 because two West African countries grow most of the world's supply and both had bad weather in the same season. The chocolate aisle is downstream of rainfall in Ghana.
texte:
In April 2024 the price of cocoa on the New York and London futures exchanges briefly cleared US$12,000 per tonne. The commodity had traded at roughly US$2,500 for most of the preceding decade and had been at about US$4,000 as recently as January of the same year, which means the price close to tripled in the space of a season. Nothing in the demand side had changed. The chocolate industry had not suddenly started using more cocoa, and consumers had not suddenly started eating more chocolate.
What had changed was that Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, the two neighbouring West African countries that together grow about 60 per cent of the world’s cocoa beans, had both had a bad growing season at the same time. The Ghana Cocoa Board’s official 2023-24 harvest came in at 425,000 tonnes, a 22-year low and roughly half of what had been forecast twelve months earlier. Côte d’Ivoire’s crop fell by about 21 per cent to its lowest level in eight years. Between them the two countries produced somewhere in the region of 500,000 tonnes less cocoa than the world had expected, and the world’s chocolate manufacturers had to bid for what remained.
Why the supply is that concentrated
Cocoa is a tropical understory tree native to the western Amazon, and it grows commercially only in a narrow belt within about 20 degrees of the equator, where the temperature stays in a specific range and the rainfall lands in a specific pattern. Par Fanny Noaro-Kabré
En Côte d'Ivoire, un syndicat de producteurs de cacao appelle à une « grève illimitée » depuis mercredi 16 septembre 2026. Il entend dénoncer les conditions de rémunération des cacaoculteurs, alors que la nouvelle campagne de commercialisation a démarré il y a deux semaines dans le pays, le 1eᣴ septembre. Un mouvement qui semble toutefois très peu suivi.
L'un des points de crispation pour le Syndicat national agricole pour le progrès en Côte d'Ivoire (Synap-CI) est le prix fixé pour la nouvelle campagne : 1 200 francs CFA le kilo bord-champ, soit une baisse de plus de 60 % par rapport à l'an dernier.
Le syndicat affirme également qu'un stock résiduel de la dernière campagne demeure. Une déclaration en contradiction avec celle du Conseil Café-Cacao qui, le 5 août, avait annoncé avoir racheté 100 000 tonnes de cacao stockées, conformément aux objectifs fixés. Le président du Synap-CI, Moussa Koné, dit avoir donné pour consigne aux producteurs de « garder le cacao récolté dans les plantations, et de ne pas l'acheminer vers les ports pour exportation ».

Cumulative shipments from Ivory Coast farmers to ports reached 2.14 million metric tons in the current marketing year running from October 1, 2025, through September 13, 2026, up 18% from the same period a year ago.
Ivory Coast cocoa regulator Le Conseil du Café Cacao separately reported that the country harvested 2.06 million metric tons of cocoa from June 2025 to June 2026, a 30% increase from 1.58 million metric tons a year earlier.

A box of bonbons that costs a little more this season, a chocolate croissant edging up in price, a shorter run of winter truffles: in New York, cocoa’s global price surge arrives in small, very local ways. As recovering global demand and tighter supply have pushed cocoa prices higher, Manhattan shoppers are seeing the pressure show up first in the city’s bakeries, cafés, and specialty chocolate counters.
How a Global Crop Story Reaches New York
Cocoa is traded on an international market, so New York chocolate makers buy into a price system shaped far from the city. The recent cocoa price surge, driven by recovering global demand and supply concerns in major producing countries in West Africa, has kept costs unusually unsettled.
Cocoa futures provide one way to track how expectations around future supply and demand are changing, with historical and live market data available through financial platforms such as TradingView. When prices become volatile, small food businesses can eventually feel the effects even if their neighborhood shop looks unchanged at first glance.
For Manhattan makers, that volatility lands on top of already steep costs. Rent, labor, utilities, packaging, and freight were never minor line items here, so a jump in cocoa rarely acts alone. It becomes one more pressure point in a city where every ingredient decision is tied to a tight margin.

Ghana’s cocoa export revenue nearly doubled in 2025, but the sharp increase has triggered questions over how much of the additional value generated from the commodity reached farmers.
The Institute of Economic Research and Public Policy (IERPP) says the widening gap between Ghana’s cocoa export earnings and the producer price paid to farmers warrants a detailed review of the financial flows across the cocoa value chain.

Citrus Greening has plagued Florida farmers for decades.
According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, since the disease was first detected, Florida's citrus production has dropped by almost 95%.
But a newly developed tree approved for rollout last week could be the potential solution.
It's called CarriCea T1, and is a rootstock that University of Florida researchers developed that resists citrus greening.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency approved the company Soilicea to sell more than 300,000 of these trees.
Mingder Yang is the assistant director of UF Innovate, the school's technology commercialization office which licensed these new rootstocks.

Citrus Greening has plagued Florida farmers for decades.
According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, since the disease was first detected, Florida's citrus production has dropped by almost 95%.
But a newly developed tree approved for rollout last week could be the potential solution.
It's called CarriCea T1, and is a rootstock that University of Florida researchers developed that resists citrus greening.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency approved the company Soilicea to sell more than 300,000 of these trees.
Mingder Yang is the assistant director of UF Innovate, the school's technology commercialization office which licensed these new rootstocks.
He said this approach is revolutionary because it offers an alternative method to protect against citrus greening.
The usual remedy? Yang said farmers inject their trees with antibiotics, but that can be costly and time consuming.
" People are trying all different type of things. Try and find beneficial bacteria to combat it. Nothing has so far proven a long-term success or economic beneficial for the growers. And this is a more permanent solution, if you will," Yang said.
Yang said the next step is to see — over time — how well these new trees fight off citrus greening and how well they bear fruits.

titre: Africa: El Niño and Disease Threaten West Africa's Cocoa Harvest
texte:
Africa: El Niño and Disease Threaten West Africa's Cocoa Harvest
1 September 2026
Daba Finance (Abidjan)
Cocoa prices are rising as disease, weak pod development and the return of El Niño threaten the next harvest in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, which together account for more than half of global supply. New York cocoa reached an 11-month high as traders focused on risks to the 2026/27 crop.
Ghana's Cocoa Board estimates production at 650,000 metric tons for 2026/27, down 13% from 750,000 tons this season. Farmers are dealing with black pod disease, swollen shoot disease and aging trees. Heavy rain and limited sunshine have also reduced pod development and made it harder to control fungal infections.
The outlook in Côte d'Ivoire is also weaker. Early crop surveys point to production of about 1.8 million tons in the season starting in September, down 18% from about 2.2 million tons in 2025/26. Poor pod formation and weather have raised concerns about the main crop, while some exporters expect arrivals to ports to start later than usual.
El Niño adds another risk. The weather pattern can bring warmer and drier conditions to West Africa, reducing soil moisture and cocoa yields. StoneX cut its forecast for the 2026/27 global cocoa surplus to 25,000 tons from 149,000 tons, while Transgraph Consulting expects the surplus to shrink to 80,000 tons from 415,000 tons.

texte:
Cote d'Ivoire aims to boost cocoa processing amid price drop
ABIDJAN, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Cote d'Ivoire plans to expand local cocoa processing to capture more value from the sector as farmgate prices fall sharply, authorities said Tuesday.
Cote d'Ivoire expects its installed cocoa processing capacity to increase from the current 1.155 million tonnes to 1.344 million tonnes during the 2026-2027 season, following the commissioning of new industrial processing plants, said Yves Brahima Kone, director general of the Coffee and Cocoa Board, at the opening of the 10th edition of the National Cocoa and Chocolate Days in Abidjan.
The increase in capacity is part of the efforts to develop local processing, increase the added-value generated in the country, and strengthen the competitiveness of the cocoa sector.
Cote d'Ivoire processed 650,000 tonnes of cocoa during the 2025-2026 season, representing a processing rate of around 30 percent, Kone said.
Kone also stressed the need to increase investment in research to develop high-yielding seeds, disease- and drought-resistant plants, as well as solutions to promote the mechanization of agricultural operations and improve the phytosanitary protection of cocoa plantations.
The push to expand processing comes as cocoa farmers face a sharp drop in farmgate prices.

titre: From cocoa to pistachios: Confectionery fraud surges as manufacturers fight to keep up
texte:
Confectionery fraud: overview
Confectionery fraud is rising globally
Risks span cocoa, nuts, honey, colours, flavours and gelatine ingredients
Ingredient substitution and false claims occur throughout supply chains
Fraud increasingly threatens consumer safety through undeclared allergens and mislabelling
Manufacturers combine testing, traceability and audits to reduce risks
Cases of confectionery fraud are growing worldwide, with rising cocoa prices, supply chain disruptions and increasing demand for premium ingredients creating stronger incentives for economically motivated adulteration.
And fraud can take many forms, including the substitution of cocoa butter with cheaper vegetable fats, the dilution of honey and sweeteners with low-cost syrups, counterfeit branded chocolates, and the misrepresentation of ingredient origin or quality claims.
What’s more, fraud opportunities are emerging at multiple points throughout the confectionery supply chain, with experts warning that understanding where those vulnerabilities exist is crucial to managing risk.
Confectionery at risk
According to public health and safety organisation NSF, confectionery fraud falls into three main categories – upstream, mid-chain and downstream.

This season, the European Union has imported a record-breaking 1,572,564 tons of citrus, marking the highest level on record. This information comes from a report published Wednesday by the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Food (MAPA), based on data from September 2025 to May 2026.
The report attributes the all-time high to September shipments from South Africa and ongoing shipments from Turkey and Egypt since the beginning of the year. The volume surpasses the cumulative total for the same period in the 2022–2023 season, which was previously the highest, and amounts to 1,564.3 million euros, the highest in recent seasons. This is a 16.4% increase over the total from September to May of last season, and 30.8% above the average of the last five seasons.
The report highlights a notable rise in imports of small citrus fruits like clementines and mandarins, which increased by 55.4% in volume -reaching a record high- and also an 8.6% increase in orange imports. South Africa remains the top citrus supplier, holding a 31.4% market share and increasing volumes by 27.8% compared to the five-year average. Egypt ranks second, with a 31% rise above average, while Turkey falls to third with slightly below-average volumes. Morocco ranks fourth, with a 7.3% growth.

titre: Berkane soft citrus harvest approaches with stable volumes expected
texte:

The first harvests of soft citrus from Morocco's Berkane region (east) are expected to begin soon, with mandarins and clementines both on track for their usual windows. According to Mohamed Saiidi of Verger Domaine Tarifit and packing house Eurober, volumes are expected to hold steady compared to the previous year, with room for a slight increase, citing "similar production conditions."
"The first soft citrus harvests from the Berkane region are approaching, with Mandarins arriving at the end of September, followed by clementines in October. Climate conditions remain very similar to those of the previous season, but we're doing much better when it comes to water supply following the country's emergence from drought."
Growers in the region faced a significant heatwave in the previous days. Saaidi describes the situation: "Between August 7th and 15th, we experienced an intense heatwave, with temperatures reaching 44°C. There was some fruit drop as a result, but the impact on expected volumes will be limited. Growers were able to adapt through more intensive irrigation."
This adaptability, he says, is a direct product of an improved water situation compared to the previous years. "So far, we are comfortable with our water supply. Irrigation is no longer a concern, unlike last year."

Slumping cocoa price leaves West Africa's farmers struggling to comply with EU's anti-deforestation law – EUobserver
texte:
Tumbling cocoa prices risk slowing preparations for the EU’s deforestation regulation (EUDR), as farmers and industry groups struggle to bear the costs of new measures to trace where cocoa beans were produced.
The price of a tonne of cocoa peaked at $12,000 (€10,360) in 2024, when the EUDR was initially supposed to come into force, but has slumped to around $3,000 (€2,600), a fall of some 80 percent.
Earlier this year, Ghana’s finance minister, Cassiel Ato Forson, announced a nearly 30 percent cut in the wholesale price that farmers receive, from around €290 per 64-kilogram bag to €210.
Ghana is the world’s second largest producer of cocoa and the price collapse has also hit the industry body, COCOBOD, which owes around €800m to the country’s cocoa farmers.
Traders have estimated that in 2025/26 there was a global surplus of 365,000 tonnes, with the Ivory Coast and Ghana reporting hefty and growing stockpiles of cocoa beans.
But at the same time, authorities are still rolling out tracing regimes across the four West African states – Ivory Coast, Ghana, Nigeria, and Cameroon – which together produce around 75 percent of the world’s cocoa and send about two-thirds of their exports to the EU.
In Nigeria, where about 300,000 mostly small-scale farmers produce cocoa, industry experts estimate that less than half national production could meet the EU requirements when the rules take effect at the end of December.

titre: Oil prices rose – Shafaqna English | International Shia News & Fatwas
texte:
Shafaqna English– Crude oil prices experienced an upward movement at the start of the trading week on Monday, driven primarily by escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
Market sentiment was notably influenced by two key factors: first, the diminishing prospects for a diplomatic resolution between the United States and Iran, which has dampened hopes for a potential easing of sanctions or supply increases; and second, the observable reduction in oil tanker transit volumes through the strategically critical Strait of Hormuz.
These developments have collectively reignited concerns among traders regarding potential supply disruptions, thereby reinforcing the geopolitical risk premium that has been embedded in oil prices in recent weeks.
Brent crude futures climbed by as much as 1%, reaching a peak of $89.40 per barrel during the trading session. By 02:29 GMT, the contract was trading at $89.20, reflecting a gain of 72 cents from its previous closing price.
